source.title: Reasoning Does Not Necessarily Improve Role-Playing Ability
source.authors: Xiachong Feng; Longxu Dou; Lingpeng Kong

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream role-playing benchmark performance across model sizes, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal training allocations.
record.gate_note: The study does not report pretraining loss, training-token or compute sweeps, compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or small-run fits predicting larger runs. Its model-scale results concern downstream role-playing performance, so they bear on V6 only. Detailed per-model and sub-dataset scores are presented in the cited tables and figures; the rows below capture the paper's explicitly stated aggregate scaling findings.
record.test_reason: The study compares downstream role-playing benchmark scores across existing instruct models of different sizes (0.5B–72B, several families) and states a 'role-playing scaling law'. This is a new downstream setting bearing on V6. Scale is confounded with model family and training recipe. No loss, compute or token sweeps and no fitted curves are reported, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: role-playing performance generally rises with model size except on InCharacter, but gains are modest and inconsistent. CoT and reasoning-optimized models further disrupt the trend.
record.recipe_differences: Compares downstream role-playing scores across existing models and reasoning conditions; it does not measure held-out next-token loss, sweep training tokens or compute, or fit loss scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling pattern varies by benchmark and role-playing method; InCharacter is an exception, and CoT or reasoning-optimized models weaken the trend.
record.problems: The scaling evidence is for downstream role-playing scores, not pretraining loss; the authors describe gains as modest and inconsistent. No uncertainty estimates are stated in the reported scaling findings.
record.rows_left_out: Per-model and sub-dataset score results in Figures 1–4 and Tables 4–13 are not itemized here; the rows record the aggregate scaling findings explicitly described in Section 4.3, including the reported benchmark exception and method-dependent variation.

untested.parts: No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or regimes analysed for power-law form.
Prediction from pretraining loss, and any quantitative fit of downstream score versus scale.

missing.what: Per-model numeric scores by size within each family (e.g. Qwen2.5 0.5B–72B series per benchmark). Rows R1–R5 currently carry only a shared sentence.
Fine-grained CharacterEval dimensions by model size (e.g. Qwen2.5 behavior 1.29 to 2.65)

record.verdict_notes: Scale here is the parameter count of off-the-shelf models from different families, not a controlled scaling sweep. Training data and compute are uncontrolled, so the evidence for V6 is weak and observational. The 'scaling law' is not quantified by any fit.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Predictions from power-law fits on small runs.
Compute-optimal allocation and its scaling with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests downstream role-playing benchmark scores against model scale, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or fit quantitative predictive scaling curves.
The study does not compare power-law exponents, fitting choices, or compute-optimal splits.

relationships.condition: Direct zero-shot instruct models on CroSS-MR, SocialBench and CharacterEval
relationships.reason: Scores rise substantially with size within the Qwen2.5 and Llama families (R1, R3, R4). This is a qualitative trend only; no fitted curve is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased substantially with model size across CroSS-MR, SocialBench, and CharacterEval, without a fitted scaling curve.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot HPD and RoleBench; CoT prompting; reasoning-optimized models
relationships.reason: Gains are small or non-monotone: RoleBench Qwen2.5-72B scores 3.21 vs 21.89 at 14B. Under CoT and reasoning models, the authors say scaling is weaker and less predictable (R2, R5, R7, R8).
relationships.display_finding: RoleBench scores fell from 21.89 at Qwen2.5-14B to 3.21 at 72B, and scaling was weaker and less predictable with CoT prompting and reasoning-optimized models.

relationships.reason: No size trend; the authors state InCharacter is the exception (R6).
relationships.display_finding: Performance showed no size trend, making InCharacter an exception among the evaluated benchmarks.
